passages.t: Honest courts, and an enemy's donkey
passages.happening:
“You shall not spread a false report. Do not join the wicked by being a malicious witness” (verse 1). “You shall not follow the crowd in wrongdoing” (verse 2). “And do not show favoritism to a poor man in his lawsuit” (verse 3).

“If you encounter your enemy’s stray ox or donkey, you must return it to him” (verse 4). “If you see the donkey of one who hates you fallen under its load, do not leave it there; you must help him with it” (verse 5).

“You shall not deny justice to the poor in their lawsuits” (verse 6). “Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous” (verse 8). “Do not oppress a foreign resident, since you yourselves know how it feels to be foreigners; for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
These laws picture the village court at the town gate. Elders heard cases there, and ordinary men served as witnesses. Justice was fragile in a place like that. A false report, the pressure of a crowd, a bribe, or sympathy for one side could tip a verdict. The law forbids every one of them.

It even forbids favoring the poor (verse 3). That may surprise a reader, since the law protects the poor so often. But justice must be fair to everyone, and pity is not a reason to bend it. Two verses later the law says the opposite danger too: do not deny the poor their justice. The scale must be level both ways.

In the middle of these court laws come two about an enemy's animal. If his ox wanders, take it back. If his donkey falls under its load, help him lift it. The law carries justice out of the courtroom into the road, where a feud could easily turn into quiet neglect. You may have a quarrel with a man. You may not let his animal suffer for it.

Behind every judge stands God: ‘I will not acquit the guilty’ (verse 7).

Verse 9 repeats the law about the foreigner from 22:21 and adds something. The Hebrew says, word for word, that Israel knows the soul of the stranger. They know from inside what it is like.
passages.later:
Leviticus says the same about the courts: “you must not show partiality to the poor or favoritism to the rich; you are to judge your neighbor fairly” (Leviticus 19:15). Amos accused the leaders of his day of doing just what this law forbids: “You oppress the righteous by taking bribes; you deprive the poor of justice in the gate” (Amos 5:12).

Proverbs takes kindness to an enemy further: “If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat” (Proverbs 25:21). Paul quotes it (Romans 12:20), and Jesus says, “love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44).
passages.asks: The law asked Israel to lift an enemy's fallen donkey. Ask what concrete good you could do for someone you are at odds with. And ask whether you have ever gone along with a crowd, at work, online or in church, in saying something you did not know was true.

passages.t: Rest for the land, the servant and the stranger
passages.happening:
“For six years you are to sow your land and gather its produce, but in the seventh year you must let it rest and lie fallow, so that the poor among your people may eat from the field and the wild animals may consume what they leave” (verses 10-11). The same holds for vineyards and olive groves.

“For six days you are to do your work, but on the seventh day you must cease, so that your ox and your donkey may rest and the son of your maidservant may be refreshed, as well as the foreign resident” (verse 12).

“You must not invoke the names of other gods; they must not be heard on your lips” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Here are two sevens. Every seventh year the land rests. Every seventh day the people rest.

Notice the reason given for each. It is not first about the landowner. The fallow year is ‘so that the poor among your people may eat’, and even the wild animals. The Sabbath day is so that the ox and the donkey can rest, and the servant's son, and the foreigner. Rest is given to those who could never take it for themselves.

‘Refreshed’ translates a Hebrew verb that means to take breath. A servant gets his breath back.

The Sabbath was first given with the manna (16:23-30) and then in the Ten Commandments (20:8-11). Christians differ on how to keep a Sabbath today. The note on Exodus 16 sets out the main views, and these notes take no side.
passages.later:
Leviticus calls the seventh year “a Sabbath of complete rest for the land” (Leviticus 25:4). Deuteronomy adds the cancelling of debts: “At the end of every seven years you must cancel debts” (Deuteronomy 15:1).

Jesus said, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27).
passages.asks: God's rest was meant to reach the servant, the stranger and the animal. Ask who works so that you can rest, and whether they get rest too. And ask what it would mean for you to stop, and trust God with what you did not finish.

passages.happening:
“Three times a year you are to celebrate a feast to Me” (verse 14).

The Feast of Unleavened Bread, in the month of Abib, “because that was the month you came out of Egypt. No one may appear before Me empty-handed” (verse 15). The Feast of Harvest, with the firstfruits of the field. And the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year (verse 16).

“Three times a year all your males are to appear before the Lord GOD” (verse 17).

“Bring the best of the firstfruits of your soil to the house of the LORD your God. You must not cook a young goat in its mother’s milk” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
These three feasts follow the farming year of Canaan.

Unleavened Bread fell in the month of Abib, March to April, when the barley ripened, and it remembered the exodus. Harvest came about seven weeks later at the wheat harvest. It is called the Feast of Weeks in 34:22, and later Pentecost. Ingathering came in the autumn, when grapes and olives were brought in. It was later called Booths or Tabernacles.

A short early Hebrew inscription called the Gezer Calendar, from around the tenth century BC, lists the months of a farmer's year by their work. It begins with two months of ingathering, the same word used for this autumn feast.

The Hebrew word for a feast here, chag, means a pilgrimage festival. Three times a year scattered farmers gathered as one people before God. The rhythm of the harvest was tied to the memory of their rescue, and no one came empty-handed.

Verse 19 forbids cooking a young goat in its mother's milk. The law never says why. Some think it avoided a pagan rite, though the old theory linking it to a text from Ugarit is now widely doubted. Others see respect for the bond between mother and young, like the law about a mother bird. Others see a refusal to mix the food of life with death. Rabbinic tradition built on this verse the full separation of meat and dairy in Jewish food laws.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy names the three feasts: “at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Tabernacles” (Deuteronomy 16:16), and repeats the goat law (Deuteronomy 14:21).

The feasts became the calendar of the Gospels. Jesus died at Passover and Unleavened Bread. The Spirit came “When the day of Pentecost came” (Acts 2:1). At the Feast of Tabernacles Jesus called out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink” (John 7:37). Paul calls the risen Christ “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20).
passages.asks: No one was to come before God empty-handed, and the best of the firstfruits went first. Ask what your calendar says about what matters most to you. And ask whether you come to God with the first and best, or with what is left over.

passages.t: The angel who bears God's name
passages.happening:
“Behold, I am sending an angel before you to protect you along the way and to bring you to the place I have prepared” (verse 20). “Pay attention to him and listen to his voice; do not defy him, for he will not forgive rebellion, since My Name is in him” (verse 21).

If they obey, “I will be an enemy to your enemies and a foe to your foes” (verse 22). They must not bow to the gods of the land (verse 24). “So you shall serve the LORD your God, and He will bless your bread and your water. And I will take away sickness from among you” (verse 25). “No woman in your land will miscarry or be barren; I will fulfill the number of your days” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
The laws are finished, and the chapter turns to the road ahead. God promises to guide his people to the land by an angel. The Hebrew word, malakh, means a messenger. It can name a human envoy or a heavenly one.

This messenger is no ordinary one. ‘My Name is in him.’ In the Bible God's name stands for his presence and his character. So to defy this angel is to defy God.

Then come the blessings of obedience: bread and water, health, children and long life. These are covenant promises to the whole people in the land, the blessings of a nation that keeps faith with God.
passages.later:
Later the angel of the LORD speaks to Israel in the land and accuses them of the very thing this chapter warns against: “you are not to make a covenant with the people of this land” (Judges 2:2).

Malachi, whose name means ‘my messenger’, promises “Behold, I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me” (Malachi 3:1), and the Gospels apply it to John the Baptist.

Paul writes that God has given Jesus “the name above all names” (Philippians 2:9).
passages.hard:
Who is the angel in whom God's name dwells?

Interpreters give three main answers. Many Christian readers since the early church have identified him with the angel of the LORD who speaks as God himself in Genesis 16 and 22 and at the burning bush, and have seen in him an appearance of the Son before he became man. Others, Jewish and Christian, understand a created angel carrying God's authority, as an ambassador carries his king's name; he cannot overlook rebellion against the one who sent him. Still others read the angel as a way of speaking of God's own presence going before Israel. That fits chapter 33, where God says he will send only an angel, and Moses pleads for God himself to go with them (33:2-3, 14-15).

The text does not settle the question, and these notes do not choose. Its point does not depend on settling it: to disobey this angel is to disobey God.

A word on verse 26. It is a promise to the nation in the covenant. It is not a verdict on any woman who loses a child or cannot have one. When the disciples asked whose sin had caused a man's blindness, Jesus answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3).

If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment. God knows your story too. Please talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: God promised to go before his people on the road. Ask whose voice you are listening to as you go into what is ahead of you. And ask what other gods, of money, safety or approval, you are tempted to bow to along the way.

passages.happening:
“I will send My terror ahead of you and throw into confusion every nation you encounter” (verse 27). “I will send the hornet before you to drive the Hivites and Canaanites and Hittites out of your way” (verse 28).

“I will not drive them out before you in a single year; otherwise the land would become desolate and wild animals would multiply against you. Little by little I will drive them out ahead of you, until you become fruitful and possess the land” (verses 29-30).

The borders will reach “from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the desert to the Euphrates” (verse 31). “You shall make no covenant with them or with their gods” (verse 32), “For if you serve their gods, it will surely be a snare to you” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
These verses look ahead to Israel's entry into Canaan. The nations named were the peoples of Canaan as Israel remembered them. The Hittites here are probably groups living in Canaan by that name, not the great Hittite empire far to the north.

God says he will drive them out ‘little by little’. If the land were emptied at once, it would go wild before Israel could fill it. God's slowness is a form of care.

The ‘hornet’ is found only here and in two other places. It may be a real swarm of stinging insects, or a picture of panic, like the terror of verse 27.

The borders of verse 31 are ideal limits. They were reached only under Solomon.

The deepest danger in the land would not be its armies. It would be its gods. Israel must make no covenant with the gods of the land, because they would be ‘a snare’.
passages.later:
Joshua later says, “I sent the hornet ahead of you, and it drove out the two Amorite kings before you, but not by your own sword or bow” (Joshua 24:12). Under Solomon, “Solomon reigned over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines” (1 Kings 4:21).

Deuteronomy warns Israel not to think the land was a reward for its goodness: “It is not because of your righteousness or uprightness of heart that you are going in to possess their land” (Deuteronomy 9:5).
passages.hard:
Why does God promise to drive out the peoples of Canaan?

Many readers find these promises, and the wars that Deuteronomy and Joshua later describe, among the hardest parts of the Bible, and they are right to feel the weight. On the Bible's own account, God waited generations before this judgment: “for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete” (Genesis 15:16). Deuteronomy says it was not because Israel was better. Israel is held to the same standard, and the same snare would catch Israel too. And the line is not drawn by blood: Rahab of Jericho joins Israel, and “she has lived among the Israelites to this day” (Joshua 6:25).

These notes say nothing against any people, ancient or modern. The peoples named here are not a name for anyone living today, and this passage gives no one permission to hate or harm any people or to claim any land.
passages.asks: God gave his people what they needed at a pace they could bear. Ask where God's slowness in your life might be care rather than neglect. And ask what snare, some loyalty that competes with God, you have made peace with instead of removing.
